clinicalPearls: Duodenal atresia is a congenital obstruction of the duodenum that typically presents in the first day or two of life with bilious vomiting and upper abdominal fullness with a scaphoid lower abdomen
Vomiting is usually bilious because most obstructions lie distal to the ampulla of Vater, though a proximal lesion can cause non-bilious vomiting
The classic radiographic finding is the double-bubble sign, two gas-filled bubbles from the distended stomach and proximal duodenum with little or no distal bowel gas in complete atresia
There is a strong association with Down syndrome, so a genetic evaluation should be considered, and with other anomalies such as cardiac, renal, and other gastrointestinal defects
Polyhydramnios is common antenatally because the obstruction prevents normal swallowing and absorption of amniotic fluid
Initial management is stabilisation with gastric decompression, correction of fluid and electrolyte disturbance, and evaluation for associated anomalies before definitive surgical repair
A partial obstruction from a duodenal web or stenosis may present later and more subtly with intermittent vomiting and feeding difficulty
reference.pathophysiology: Duodenal atresia is thought to arise from failure of recanalisation of the duodenal lumen during early embryonic development, when the normally solid cord of proliferating epithelium fails to reopen. This produces a spectrum from complete atresia to a stenosis or a fenestrated web (windsock deformity). The obstruction is most often located near the ampulla of Vater, and because it is usually distal to the bile duct opening the vomiting is characteristically bilious. Proximal bowel becomes distended while distal bowel is decompressed, giving the double-bubble appearance. The developmental timing overlaps with that of other structures, which accounts for the frequent association with Down syndrome and with cardiac, renal, and other gastrointestinal anomalies.
additionalDifferentials: Malrotation with midgut volvulus, which is a surgical emergency to exclude
Annular pancreas causing extrinsic duodenal obstruction
Duodenal web or stenosis with partial obstruction
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis presenting with non-bilious vomiting
Meconium ileus or other distal bowel obstruction
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal radiograph to demonstrate the double-bubble sign and assess distal gas
Antenatal ultrasound findings of polyhydramnios and a double bubble
Upper gastrointestinal contrast study when malrotation must be excluded or the diagnosis is uncertain
Echocardiography and renal ultrasound to screen for associated anomalies
Chromosomal analysis for trisomy 21 when clinically indicated
Electrolytes and blood gas to characterise dehydration and metabolic disturbance
redFlags: Bilious vomiting in a neonate, which mandates urgent exclusion of malrotation with volvulus
Signs of bowel ischaemia such as abdominal tenderness, distension, or bloody stool
Severe dehydration and electrolyte or acid-base disturbance from persistent vomiting
Coexisting critical congenital heart disease or other major anomaly affecting stability
reference.prognosis: With timely diagnosis and surgical correction the outlook for isolated duodenal atresia is very good and most infants achieve normal feeding and growth. Prognosis is influenced mainly by prematurity and by associated anomalies, particularly complex congenital heart disease and the syndromic burden in Down syndrome.
pitfalls: Assuming bilious vomiting is benign and not urgently excluding malrotation with volvulus
Missing a partial obstruction from a duodenal web that presents late with subtle symptoms
Overlooking associated cardiac, renal, or chromosomal conditions before surgery
Delaying gastric decompression and fluid resuscitation while awaiting definitive imaging
Attributing the double-bubble sign solely to duodenal atresia without considering annular pancreas or malrotation
references: Cloherty and Stark Manual of Neonatal Care
management: Stabilise the neonate first with nasogastric or orogastric decompression to relieve the proximal obstruction and prevent aspiration
Correct fluid and electrolyte disturbance and any metabolic derangement before surgery
Undertake definitive surgical repair, typically duodenoduodenostomy, to restore intestinal continuity
Screen for associated anomalies with echocardiography and renal ultrasound, and exclude malrotation with a contrast study where the diagnosis is uncertain
Support nutrition postoperatively with parenteral feeding, transitioning to enteral feeds as gastrointestinal function returns
Manage within a multidisciplinary neonatal, paediatric surgical, cardiology and genetics team
Arrange chromosomal analysis for trisomy 21 and offer genetic counselling given the strong Down syndrome association
